claims.statement: The static-scanning pipeline has four scanners — Semgrep over the TS/JS and Python source surfaces, cargo-audit over the root Cargo.lock, pnpm audit over pnpm-lock.yaml, and pip-audit over the Python venvs — whose output is normalized into one findings report consumed by a single blocking `sast` job in the guardrails workflow.

The `sast` gate blocks only on findings where severity is High or Critical AND the finding is either SAST kind or runtime-scope SCA; Medium/Low findings and dev-scope SCA findings are warnings that never fail the gate.

The SCA half of the scan runs full on every run and is deliberately not path-gated, because a newly published advisory can affect an unchanged dependency; consequently `main` can legitimately go red on a dependency nobody touched.

On pull requests the scan uses `--scope changed` with an explicit Semgrep target list, so the extension filter in `isScanTarget()` — not a rule's own `paths:` — decides what a pull request is gated on; workflow YAML and Dockerfiles were each added to that filter only after a finding reached `main` ungated.

`check-sast-findings.mjs` has a second, distinct blocking exit path, `GATE-SCOPE ASYMMETRY`: on a full-scope report, any blocking SAST finding whose file `isScanTarget()` rejects fails the gate with its own section, counting suppressed findings too, excluding SCA and changed-scope reports, and throwing a hard error when the report has no usable `generatedAtScope`.

The gate-symmetry check's only exemption is the explicit `reportAbsent` marker the gate synthesises when no SAST report exists at all — the case of the weekly expiry run in the infra-image-scan job — never a missing `generatedAtScope` field on a report that exists.

Since feature 068 pip-audit audits four Python surfaces (agents/movie-assistant plus three mcp-servers), each deriving its own dependency and runtime sets, and a Python project carrying a `uv.lock` that is absent from `PYTHON_SURFACES` fails the scan rather than being silently omitted or silently auto-included.

pip-audit findings are project-qualified (`mcp-servers/web-api-mcp:click@8.5.0`), so the same advisory in two surfaces yields separately suppressible findings, and `assertPipAuditAllowlistShape` statically rejects an anchored `locationPattern` naming a surface that does not exist because such an entry can never match.

pip-audit audits the installed venv rather than a requirements file, so an unsynced surface fails the whole scan — never reporting three-of-four as success — and CI must `uv sync` all four surfaces before the scan runs.
Every scanner is keyless and fail-closed: rule and advisory data are fetched anonymously at scan time and any fetch failure fails the job instead of producing a false clean, with no secret required.

`p/secrets` is deliberately absent from the Semgrep config because `secret-scan.mjs` is the sole owner of credential detection; enabling it here would double-gate and split the allowlist across two owners.

Rust source code is outside Semgrep's scope — clippy owns Rust source patterns and cargo-audit covers only Rust dependencies — so the mc-service Rust surface relies on clippy plus review for the invariants Semgrep enforces on TS/JS and Python.

Semgrep resolves its five `p/*` community packs from its public registry at scan time, so with that host blocked it fails closed and leaves an empty `findings.json` that the gate passes vacuously; the host is in the committed egress allowlist but the host-side sandbox policy is per-sandbox and needs an operator re-application, so the committed entry alone does not establish reachability.

Because the empty-report green is specific to Semgrep, `--only pnpm-audit` (and the other SCA scanners) still produces a real local report — which matters because every dependency-floor remediation is an SCA finding — and the report's finding COUNT, not the exit code, is what distinguishes a vacuous pass from a clean scan.

A Semgrep rule it could not RUN appears in the native `errors[]` and never in `results[]`, contributing zero findings so its allowlist entry reads as remediated; the orchestrator groups those errors per rule into `blindedRules` and the gate prints them as `RULES THAT COULD NOT RUN`, annotating an `UNMATCHED` entry whose rule is in that list.

The blinded-rule attribution must read the rule name out of the error message prose as well as the structured `rule_id` field, because the pinned Semgrep populates that field on `Internal matching error` but not on `PartialParsing` errors — keying on the field alone understated 36 errors as 3.

`node scripts/sast-scan.mjs --test-rules` runs `semgrep --test` over `security/sast/rules/` and additionally fails on a rule with no fixture, because `semgrep --test` silently skips an unfixtured rule and still reports all tests passing; the Semgrep pin lives only in `sast-scan.mjs`.

A `sast` gate failure whose output says `TRANSPORT/SERVICE ERROR` is a third-party outage that survived three bounded retries and should be re-run, not read as a finding: pip-audit queries osv.dev, cargo-audit fetches the RustSec advisory DB, and pnpm audit queries the npm registry, and the classifier distinguishes those from a real fault which still fails on the first attempt.

The transient-retry classifier is one shared module used by both `sast-scan.mjs` and `infra-image-scan.mjs`, deliberately extracted rather than copied because the hard part is the signature list, and it preserves fail-closed behaviour by re-throwing after the attempts are exhausted.

HTTP-status transient signatures require the status CODE, not just the phrase, because bare `Service Unavailable`/`Bad Gateway`/`Too Many Requests` and a bare `Read timed out` also occur in advisory titles that reach the classifier via stderr plus stdout — so a genuine finding would have been retried three times and then reported anyway.

`scripts/lib/scanner-retry.mjs` also owns the shared tail-truncation helper, so a captured scanner failure keeps its final lines — where the HTTP status is — instead of its head, which once left a digest ending mid-URL and unable to name the failure.

Keyed entries in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s `overrides:` map are a range keyed on a range where the key names the vulnerable span excluded and the value the patched floor forced; `scripts/check-override-consistency.mjs` enforces equality between the key's exclusive upper bound and the value's inclusive lower bound on pull requests, scoped to keys carrying an `@<range>` suffix while plain pins are out of scope.

Renovate cannot raise the lower bound of a keyed override — it parses `name@<range>` as an opaque depName and half-bumps when it rewrites one — which is why the override-consistency guard is needed for floor raises.

The `sast` gate prints an advisory `OVERRIDE LEVERS` section naming which lever clears a finding whose package already carries an override — `refresh-lockfile` when the range already permits the fix, `raise-floor` naming both halves when it does not — computed per resolution rather than per package and never affecting the exit code.

The pnpm `overrides` map lives in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` rather than `package.json`'s `pnpm` field because pnpm 11 stopped reading that field and warns about ignored keys; the warning is a security event because every override exists to force a vulnerable transitive dependency to a patched version.

Allowlist suppression is gate-only: a suppressed finding leaves the failure set but remains visible in the report and is printed as allowlisted by its `addedBy`; entries require scanner, id, locationPattern, justification and addedBy, and a blank required field or invalid regex is a gate error (exit 2).

Expiry classification has three states with both window boundaries inclusive, defined once as `WARNING_WINDOW_DAYS = 14` in `scripts/allowlist-expiry.mjs` and imported by both gates; only `expired` stops suppression, and classification is computed on UTC date boundaries from a caller-supplied `today` so no timezone or DST shift can move an entry between states.

Unmatched-entry detection is evaluated only for scanners that produced at least one finding in the run, so a skipped, failed or genuinely clean scanner never flags its whole entry set as stale; an entry keyed on an exact advisory id does not expire when a scanner switches identifier namespace, it just quietly stops suppressing.

The `--check-expiring` mode is report-only over blocking findings, runs twice weekly (Tuesday and Friday 04:00 UTC) in the `infra-image-scan` workflow over both allowlists, is never run on pull requests, and for the SAST allowlist cannot fail on an unmatched entry because that job produces no SAST report.

The weekly expiry step must be `always()`-guarded inside its schedule guard, because a failed step earlier in the job (the CVE gate) otherwise skips it entirely — so on the week the gate is red the expiry warning did not run at all (item #484); and a cancelled run is skipped from inside the step body via `job.status` rather than in the `if:` so a superseded run is not turned into a failure.

The report-absent path of the expiry check must announce a missing report rather than assume clean and must not throw; when it threw, the step aborted and `bash -e` skipped the following infra-image expiry check, leaving both expiry tiers dead from 2026-09-12 until the 2026-09-25 weekly sweep exposed it.

A time-boxed allowlist acceptance must be remediated rather than re-dated: deleting or extending an `expiry` is how a time-box becomes permanent, and the only legitimate exception — no published fix exists — requires the evidence written into the justification.

Allowlist `locationPattern`s are matched against paths normalized to forward slashes so one pattern is portable across the Windows dev host and the Linux CI runner; a backslash pattern matches nothing on the runner while passing silently on Windows.

Dependency scope for SCA is computed per ecosystem (cargo tree --edges no-dev, pnpm audit --prod across all workspace packages, uv export --no-dev), and a scope that cannot be computed defaults to runtime, so an unknown never silently downgrades a finding out of the blocking set.
An unmapped native severity is a hard error rather than a silent default: the orchestrator applies `security/sast/severity-map.yaml` and fails fast on a value the map does not cover.

This static scan is disjoint from DAST (which exercises the running app), from infra-image scanning (which covers pulled third-party container images rather than first-party code or first-party dependency graphs), and from `secret-scan.mjs` (the sole owner of credential detection).

The SCA `runtime` tag answers whether the whole-workspace `--prod` audit sees the package, not whether the vulnerable code path is exercised; two of the three current no-fix acceptances (node-forge, braces) are tagged runtime solely because `expo` declares `@expo/cli` a production dependency while the vulnerable code sits in Expo CLI / code-signing tooling and in micromatch under Metro's file watcher and Jest, so reachability must be checked separately and written into the justification.

A custom rule's documented limitation is triaged into the allowlist rather than worked around: `mcm-auth-before-authz` only recognizes a guard call textually earlier in the same function, so the backups reader/writer and the account-deletion pipeline — all of which receive an already-authenticated (or step-up) token from a route wrapper — carry entries pinned to those individual files, so a new unguarded upstream client anywhere else still fails the gate, and pushing a `requireMcUser` call down into those functions would contradict the role-enforcement-is-a-layer rule by reintroducing the per-call-site check that rule exists to prevent.

Where no patched version exists, the allowlist convention is to pin `locationPattern` to the exact vulnerable version and short-date the entry, so a different version re-blocks for a fresh assessment and the entry stops suppressing on its own — with the reachability check that was actually performed recorded in the justification.

A suppression that matches nothing is deleted rather than renewed or re-anchored, because a dead entry would silently absorb a genuine regression on that package until its expiry; the retired click entry and the feature-034 remediations were all discharged this way.

The `OVERRIDE LEVERS` advice is emitted only for an SCA finding whose `fixAvailable` yields a parseable floor and whose resolved version sits inside a KEYED override's range (plain pins produce nothing), is deduped per package plus resolution plus action, is printed for non-blocking findings as well as blocking ones, and an unreadable or absent `pnpm-workspace.yaml` is swallowed to an empty override map outside `gate()` so the gate's result can never depend on it.

The expiry-check and gate-scope wiring is pinned statically: exactly one step in the `infra-image-scan` job invokes `--check-expiring`, it must cover both allowlists, its `if:` must contain the schedule guard, and no other workflow may invoke `--check-expiring` at all — because a wrong guard is green today and blocks every pull request a fortnight later, while an absent override-consistency step looks identical to a passing one.
